Tagging p2p-excluded, releasing per D-002.",
        "_claimSubjectBaseline": {
          "body": "## The symptom\nThe rig (Lm1ABoMR), running a bundle that CONTAINS fix C (composedAt 2026-07-27T11:44:22Z), receives the canonical key in a refusal every single tick and never adopts it:\n\n```\n[2026-07-27T11:51:22.768Z] [git-sync] papercusp: ref-announce receive fetch FAILED for\nIXfGu216EI/z (event 441080); holding cursor at 440845 to re-dial next tick:\nno git process ran: duplex error: pot-git serve refused: superseded-repo-key:gh-1223568103\n```\n\nFive of these in a single tick. The correct canonical key `gh-1223568103` is sitting in the error text. Nothing adopts it. The rig's `papercusp.git` still holds ZERO namespaces.\n\n## The root cause — reachability, not logic\n`adoptRefusedRepoKey` is correct and well-guarded. It has exactly ONE production call site:\n\n- `git-sync-action.ts:2034` — inside the BOOTSTRAP leg's dial path.\n\nBut the refusal that carries the repair arrives on a DIFFERENT leg: the ref-announce RECEIVE leg (`git-sync-action.ts:~2345`, the `cursorDecision.fetchFailed` loop). That loop has `f.stderr` containing the verbatim refusal text — and does nothing with it but `console.warn`.\n\nSo the one channel on which the repair reliably and repeatedly arrives is the one channel that cannot act on it.\n\n## Why this is the mirror image of fix D\nFix D's own comment (git-sync-action.ts:1839) says the probe must sit ABOVE the warm gate because \"a probe placed after the gate would never fire on precisely the machine that needs it: the stuck one.\" Fix C has the same defect in a different dimension: its receiver is on the cold-join path, so it never runs on the machine whose ref-announce leg is the thing actually dialing.\n\n## The fix\nCall `adoptRefusedRepoKey` from the ref-announce receive leg's fetchFailed handler, using `f.stderr` — the same fail-soft, next-tick-effective contract the bootstrap call site already uses. Adoption is idempotent (`already-canonical` is a clean no-op on every later refused dial), so calling it from both legs is safe by construction.\n\n## Broader lesson (worth keeping)\nA REFUSAL THAT CARRIES ITS OWN REPAIR ONLY HEALS IF EVERY LEG THAT CAN RECEIVE IT KNOWS HOW TO READ IT. Wiring the receiver into one leg makes the feature look done and tested while leaving it inert on the live path.",

So the true figures are 200 affected stamps (filed: 126) and 83 with a live sibling (filed: 51) — the filer UNDER-CLAIMED by ~1.6x on both. That is the THIRD independent confirmation of D-026 s4's direction-of-error rule, on a third unrelated finding, and it is now safe to treat \"a filed number is a floor to re-measure\" as established rather than suggestive. R-related to EI-20577421906951067, not a duplicate: this one is the OVER-FIRE (things get closed that should not be), that one is the IRREVERSIBILITY (a wrong closure cannot be undone). They are two halves of one trap and neither is safe to fix alone — fixing only the over-fire leaves existing bad closures stuck; fixing only the reopen path leaves the source of them running. Until one of those lands every composition-preserving route is measured-dead and there is no agent-side work that can advance this item — a claimant would only re-derive three refuted levers. Full state + resume contract is on the checkpoint.",
          "reachability": "reachable"
        },
        "_claimSubjectBaseline": {
          "body": "DIRECT FOLLOW-UP to EI-23345472964244980 (closed 2026-09-16), which built the per-tool argSchema byte budget + the two seed wire guards and established the headline: the core MCP spine is 353,380 B in-repo against D-001's 262,144 B ceiling (34.8% over), with 8 of 48 names = 55% of it. That item MEASURED and GUARDED the breach. This one is about CUTTING it, and it starts by killing the obvious wrong answer.\n\n=== NEGATIVE RESULT FIRST — DO NOT SPEND A SESSION ON THIS ===\nThe natural fix is 'the whales inline the same nested payload twice, so switch the converter to emit $defs/$ref'. Concretely: libs/generic/tooldef/src/schema-adapter.ts calls z.toJSONSchema(schema) with NO options, and Zod 4 defaults `reused` to 'inline'. Flipping it to 'ref' looks like a one-line catalog-wide win.\n\nIT IS REFUTED, on two independent grounds, both measured 2026-09-16:\n\n1. MEASURED WORSE on the population that could be re-converted. Over the 67 tools still carrying their zod `args`, reused:'ref' produced 68,805 B vs 58,201 B inline — 18.2% BIGGER. 48 of 67 grew by exactly +51 B: the $defs wrapper overhead with no actual reuse to amortize. (That sample contains no whale, so it does not by itself settle the whales — ground 2 does.)\n\n2. STRUCTURALLY INCOMPATIBLE WITH THE PROJECTION. libs/generic/tooldef/src/define-tool.ts:1298 `flattenForOpenAi` DELIBERATELY flattens root-level oneOf/anyOf into one merged object, because LLM clients cannot accept a root union in a tool inputSchema. The projection's whole job is to FLATTEN. Emitting $defs/$ref would fight that pass, not cooperate with it. The inlining is intentional, not an oversight.\n\nAlso worth knowing for any future probe: the projected registry (listAllProjectedTools(), 889 tools) carries ONLY the already-converted `inputSchema` — zero of the 889 retain the zod `args`, so you cannot re-convert from it. The zod source survives only in the legacy getCatalog() catalog, and importing that from @papercusp/agent-mcp in a scratch probe returned just 67 tools (a different module record — the documented singleton-split trap). Measure composition from `inputSchema`; it needs no zod.\n\n=== WHERE THE BYTES ACTUALLY ARE (in-repo projection, 889 tools) ===\nTOTAL 1,216,782 B, of which DESCRIPTION PROSE = 627,429 B = 51.6%.\n\nname                          total    prose  prose%\nwork_items:complete           43,283   21,714    50%\ncoord:send                    38,185   29,305    77%\nrubrics:propose               36,402   20,074    55%\nrubrics:amend                 27,927   14,602    52%\nwork_items:checkpoint         23,358   16,477    71%\nfleet:launch-on-plan          21,940   17,421    79%\nloop:checkpoint               20,174   14,008    69%\nimprovements:capture          19,033   12,175    64%\nscorecards:emit               17,743    6,967    39%\nfacts:assert                  14,452   11,603    80%\ncapability:launch-agent       11,262    8,100    72%\nwork_items:create             10,778    6,195    57%\n\nSo the dominant lever is PROSE, not structure — and it is ungoverned: the existing tool-weight promptWeight budget measures the tool's own `description` + `guidance` fields, NOT the .describe() strings inside the argSchema. A tool can sit comfortably inside its prompt budget while shipping 29 KB of schema prose on every tools/list (coord:send does exactly that: 1,356 chars of prompt weight, 38,185 B of argSchema).\n\n=== THE MULTIPLIER, which changes the ranking ===\nwork_items:complete top-level properties: items=21,921 B, completion=17,235 B, specAdequacy=2,945 B, everything else <310 B. `completion` and `items[].completion` are the SAME completionSpec, serialized twice (single-shorthand branch + items[] batch branch, merged by flattenForOpenAi). So every byte of prose inside completionSpec is paid TWICE — a 1-char trim there saves 2 bytes. Any tool offering a single shorthand beside an items[] batch has this doubling; that is the shared shape behind several whales.\n\n=== PROPOSED WORK, cheapest and least-risky first ===\n1. TRIM PROSE in the top whales' argSchemas, prioritising the doubled nested specs (completionSpec first — 2x yield per byte). Pure prose editing: reversible, no contract change, no client-compat question, and it is the same discipline the repo already applies to tool description/guidance — prefer a docs pointer over prose-in-place. Rough ceiling if the top 12 alone went from ~65% prose to ~30%: on the order of 60-70 KB in-repo, which reads HIGHER on the wire (in-repo runs ~20-35% below live).\n2. EXTEND THE GOVERNANCE so this cannot regrow: the new SCHEMA_BYTE_BUDGET from EI-23345472964244980 caps total argSchema bytes per tool, but nothing caps the PROSE FRACTION. A prose-share signal in `npm run tool-weight` would make the 77%/80% outliers visible at edit time rather than at the gate.\n3. ONLY THEN consider de-duplicating the single/batch pairing (e.g. advertising the items[] form alone while the existing z.preprocess hoisting — hoistMisplacedCompletionFields / gatherFlatCompletion — keeps flat single calls working at runtime). Listed last deliberately.\n\nEVIDENCE: probes .papercusp/scratch/reused-ref-win.mts and .papercusp/scratch/whale-composition.mts (gitignored scratch; both re-runnable with `npx tsx <path>`, they load the agent-tools barrel and process.exit(0) — note the documented 'barrel hangs under bare tsx' is really just the barrel's listeners holding the event loop open, which the explicit exit resolves).\n\nⓘ Possible STALE RUNTIME, not an open defect: `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/work_items/complete.ts` (32 newer commits, tip `8624ebc8dc74ea542338bf1f9218922ced88bc3d`), `packages/operator-core/lib/agent-tools/coordination/tools/send.ts` (5 newer commits, tip `60fd7a89a65540dcd8da92db661aefd61222ffdf`) have commits newer than the running build (`e66be3c4ff`) in `staging`.           "kind": "change",
          "title": "51.6% of the catalog's 1.22 MB argSchema wire cost is .describe() PROSE (627 KB) — ungoverned; and the $ref fix is refuted, the lever is prose + the single/batch duplication",
          "summary": "DIRECT FOLLOW-UP to EI-23345472964244980 (closed 2026-09-16), which built the per-tool argSchema byte budget + the two seed wire guards and established the headline: the core MCP spine is 353,380 B in-repo against D-001's 262,144 B ceiling (34.8% over), with 8 of 48 names = 55% of it. That item MEASURED and GUARDED the breach. This one is about CUTTING it, and it starts by killing the obvious wrong answer.\n\n=== NEGATIVE RESULT FIRST — DO NOT SPEND A SESSION ON THIS ===\nThe natural fix is 'the whales inline the same nested payload twice, so switch the converter to emit $defs/$ref'. Concretely: libs/generic/tooldef/src/schema-adapter.ts calls z.toJSONSchema(schema) with NO options, and Zod 4 defaults `reused` to 'inline'. Flipping it to 'ref' looks like a one-line catalog-wide win.\n\nIT IS REFUTED, on two independent grounds, both measured 2026-09-16:\n\n1. MEASURED WORSE on the population that could be re-converted. Over the 67 tools still carrying their zod `args`, reused:'ref' produced 68,805 B vs 58,201 B inline — 18.2% BIGGER. 48 of 67 grew by exactly +51 B: the $defs wrapper overhead with no actual reuse to amortize. (That sample contains no whale, so it does not by itself settle the whales — ground 2 does.)\n\n2. STRUCTURALLY INCOMPATIBLE WITH THE PROJECTION. libs/generic/tooldef/src/define-tool.ts:1298 `flattenForOpenAi` DELIBERATELY flattens root-level oneOf/anyOf into one merged object, because LLM clients cannot accept a root union in a tool inputSchema. The projection's whole job is to FLATTEN. Emitting $defs/$ref would fight that pass, not cooperate with it. The inlining is intentional, not an oversight.\n\nAlso worth knowing for any future probe: the projected registry (listAllProjectedTools(), 889 tools) carries ONLY the already-converted `inputSchema` — zero of the 889 retain the zod `args`, so you cannot re-convert from it. The zod source survives only in the legacy getCatalog() catalog, and importing that from @papercusp/agent-mcp in a scratch probe returned just 67 tools (a different module record — the documented singleton-split trap). Measure composition from `inputSchema`; it needs no zod.\n\n=== WHERE THE BYTES ACTUALLY ARE (in-repo projection, 889 tools) ===\nTOTAL 1,216,782 B, of which DESCRIPTION PROSE = 627,429 B = 51.6%.\n\nname                          total    prose  prose%\nwork_items:complete           43,283   21,714    50%\ncoord:send                    38,185   29,305    77%\nrubrics:propose               36,402   20,074    55%\nrubrics:amend                 27,927   14,602    52%\nwork_items:checkpoint         23,358   16,477    71%\nfleet:launch-on-plan          21,940   17,421    79%\nloop:checkpoint               20,174   14,008    69%\nimprovements:capture          19,033   12,175    64%\nscorecards:emit               17,743    6,967    39%\nfacts:assert                  14,452   11,603    80%\ncapability:launch-agent       11,262    8,100    72%\nwork_items:create             10,778    6,195    57%\n\nSo the dominant lever is PROSE, not structure — and it is ungoverned: the existing tool-weight promptWeight budget measures the tool's own `description` + `guidance` fields, NOT the .describe() strings inside the argSchema. A tool can sit comfortably inside its prompt budget while shipping 29 KB of schema prose on every tools/list (coord:send does exactly that: 1,356 chars of prompt weight, 38,185 B of argSchema).\n\n=== THE MULTIPLIER, which changes the ranking ===\nwork_items:complete top-level properties: items=21,921 B, completion=17,235 B, specAdequacy=2,945 B, everything else <310 B. `completion` and `items[].completion` are the SAME completionSpec, serialized twice (single-shorthand branch + items[] batch branch, merged by flattenForOpenAi). So every byte of prose inside completionSpec is paid TWICE — a 1-char trim there saves 2 bytes. Any tool offering a single shorthand beside an items[] batch has this doubling; that is the shared shape behind several whales.\n\n=== PROPOSED WORK, cheapest and least-risky first ===\n1. TRIM PROSE in the top whales' argSchemas, prioritising the doubled nested specs (completionSpec first — 2x yield per byte).           "body": "The shared checkout's .git/index was truncated to zero bytes at 15:00:46Z, causing index readers to fail with 'index file smaller than expected' rather than return repository state. WI-10004909 records git-sync's declaration inventory and superproject commits blocked until read-tree rebuilt the index. WI-10004910 records a historical mutation probe rejecting a tracked file during the same index-error window; misclassifying the failed tracked-file check as 'untracked' is the inferred downstream mechanism. WI-10004911 independently confirms the zero-byte index, repeated Git failures, and doc-claims census failures that disappeared after index recovery (883/883 tests passed). The common upstream fault is the corrupt index, not missing file tracking or individual guard regressions. The truncating writer remains unidentified; coincident git-sync/bg-host activity does not establish responsibility.\n\nShared-root-cause evidence: Three current items connect the same zero-byte index incident and fatal read signature to multiple Git-backed workflows. EI-25410024981236879 and EI-25410269323486697 instead receive empty output_spill_failed envelopes. The same post-handler failure affects mutations: EI-25410122061838770 retains a recorded receipt but loses canonical output, while EI-25410344016199089 confirms a committed emit whose receipt was entirely swallowed behind retryable:true.         "_claimSubjectBaseline": {
          "body": "Bounded tool output relies on the shared result door persisting omitted bytes to scratch. EI-25428645932897748 shows a 5.3KB scorecard spill exceeding the same deadline, although its file becomes readable later, demonstrating delayed recovery rather than permanent loss in that case. EI-25428617195110357 corroborates the shared persistence/recovery boundary. Repair spill settlement and lossless overflow recovery without attributing these failures to /tmp exhaustion, quota, contention or event-loop load absent measurement.\n\nShared-root-cause evidence: Multiple current readers lose or cannot promptly recover overflow at the same result-door persistence boundary.         "_claimSubjectBaseline": {
          "body": "This item concerns intermittent failure of admin transaction startup during native session verification. The MCP rejection itself is the intentional security boundary: preserve fail-closed verification; do not admit an inherited or unverified native identity.\n\nThe original reporter recurrence was captured on 2026-10-09 against b7937697dc. A second encounter occurred during bulk-4903eb58-a140-4b78-b5da-8816ad1309f1 after four allowed acknowledgements and a 100-item recommendation batch. The transcript shows tools:invoke calling inbox:bulk-run-manifest and receiving request_rejected: superuser_native_session_verifier_unavailable before any further bulk report/action. The bulk pass subsequently completed through the sanctioned same-owner CLI route; that route's success alone did not establish native-wrapper health.\n\nThe exact second failure is tool_invocations:35038620 at 2026-10-10T01:04:07.336Z, coord owner su-7f5e54d1-974b-4603-9aeb-4cf2487f2a1d, serving process linux:b8c61f1d-f67c-43a8-ac9d-2286713e224f:38294679, build a2c76aa503. Its retained mcpAuthFailure is contextVerified=false, with carrier meta:threadId, candidateAdvSessionId=null and valueFingerprint=51d40c49bf5903be8bfae7dc1bbcf951855c4dc1c0ea365275222fc6c41ee1e0. verifierFailure.name=DbCallDeadlineError; phase=transaction_setup; acquisition.label=boundedOrgTxn:begin(admin); pool=org-admin; deadlineMs=7500; elapsedMs=7499; retryable=true. No PostgreSQL error code was retained. verifierFailure.durationMs=201 is a separate measurement from the deadline object's elapsedMs; the record does not establish that this verifier call itself waited 7499ms. The captured pool/ticket counts are seam diagnostics, not evidence of CPU/RAM exhaustion or a saturated pool.\n\nCurrent-runtime read-only probe: invoke the same manifest read through the native tools:invoke wrapper, using this session's ordinary metadata. It succeeded at 2026-10-10T01:31:59.128Z/129Z, receipts tool_invocations:35052893 (inner) and 35052894 (wrapper). Both have the EXACT SAME serving process, build a2c76aa503, carrier and native-session fingerprint as the failure, and now show binding=bound, candidateAdvSessionId=39357. adv_sessions:39357 belongs to this Codex owner and started at 2026-10-10T00:46:42.032456Z, before the failure. This establishes current binding and identity continuity; it does not retroactively authorize the rejected call. A fresh failure did not reproduce, so reproduced=true is not claimed.\n\nSecurity/source check: _mcp-host.ts:1880-1896 rejects on verifier exceptions to prevent the inherited-session authorization bug. The existing registered gating suite covers fail-closed rejection, no terminal callback dispatch, redacted diagnostics, and typed acquire/begin/setup deadline fields. Focused test run 20966201 in papercusp/local passed five selected cases; 328 cases were deliberately excluded by the name filter. Command: npm run test:file -- --require-ran packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/__tests__/mcp-handler-gating-matrix.test.ts -- '--testNamePattern=fails closed with a retryable verifier reason|retains typed .* deadline diagnostics when native verification fails closed'. The unused --require-ran token was treated as a non-test input; actual matched cases and counts are verified in testing:runs. HEAD moved 6fa9ff1f727d to b20fd572c871 during the run, runtime source capture was not configured, and the runner/ledger marked provenance unknown/worktreeDirty=true. No PostgreSQL error code was retained. verifierFailure.durationMs=201 is a separate measurement from the deadline object's elapsedMs; the record does not establish that this verifier call itself waited 7499ms.           "lastSuccessfulReproductionAt": null
        },
        "_claimSubjectBaseline": {
          "body": "Observed 2026-10-11 ~00:52Z (judge su-6b349bd0, served by build 22a41ff6e9). tools:invoke { name:'scorecards:emit' } for a grading-integrity audit returned ok:true, completionReceipt { status:'recorded', effectRef:'EI-25642263855564483' }. The response projection's spill to scratch failed with: _projection.cursor { kind:'volatile-scratch-page', reason:'spill-write-failed', errorCode:'ETIMEDOUT', errorDetail:'Error: result-door scratch spill write exceeded 30000ms' }. The full payload fell back to an in-process volatile copy (papercusp://scratch-memory/f45510f8-…, expires 00:58:18Z, lost on restart). The payload was small: originalChars 8172. A spill write of about 8KB should not take more than 30s.\n\nImpact: the write itself landed. I confirmed it with scorecards:get EI-25641616454606476: gradingAudit.state=passed, auditIssueId=EI-25642263855564483. But the emit call blocked for over 30s on the spill. And the result for a non-idempotent write was only readable from a volatile copy, so a caller with less care could repeat the emit. Earlier in the same session, code:run result-door spills succeeded. So this is intermittent and probably load-correlated. Cause unknown (unconfirmed): it could be filesystem or PG contention on the scratch store, or a serialized writer.\n\nRelated signal in the same minute: improvements:capture checkDuplicatesOnly returned dedupCoverage { lexical:'unavailable', semantic:'unavailable', degraded:true }, and the hook retrieval legs reported 'source query exceeded ~222-296ms budget'. That suggests general store latency at the time rather than a spill-specific fault. Not proven.\n\nRepro hint: emit a scorecard of about 8KB via tools:invoke under fleet load, then check _projection.cursor.reason. Suggested fix direction: make the spill write bounded or async off the response path, and add a latency metric on result-door spill writes so stalls show up in a measurement.",
          "kind": "bug",
          "title": "result-door scratch spill write exceeded 30000ms (ETIMEDOUT) on tools:invoke scorecards:emit response",
          "summary": "Observed 2026-10-11 ~00:52Z (judge su-6b349bd0, served by build 22a41ff6e9). tools:invoke { name:'scorecards:emit' } for a grading-integrity audit returned ok:true, completionReceipt { status:'recorded', effectRef:'EI-25642263855564483' }. The response projection's spill to scratch failed with: _projection.cursor { kind:'volatile-scratch-page', reason:'spill-write-failed', errorCode:'ETIMEDOUT', errorDetail:'Error: result-door scratch spill write exceeded 30000ms' }. The full payload fell back to an in-process volatile copy (papercusp://scratch-memory/f45510f8-…, expires 00:58:18Z, lost on restart). The payload was small: originalChars 8172. A spill write of about 8KB should not take more than 30s.\n\nImpact: the write itself landed. I confirmed it with scorecards:get EI-25641616454606476: gradingAudit.state=passed, auditIssueId=EI-25642263855564483. But the emit call blocked for over 30s on the spill. And the result for a non-idempotent write was only readable from a volatile copy, so a caller with less care could repeat the emit. Earlier in the same session, code:run result-door spills succeeded. So this is intermittent and probably load-correlated. Cause unknown (unconfirmed): it could be filesystem or PG contention on the scratch store, or a serialized writer.\n\nRelated signal in the same minute: improvements:capture checkDuplicatesOnly returned dedupCoverage { lexical:'unavailable', semantic:'unavailable', degraded:true }, and the hook retrieval legs reported 'source query exceeded ~222-296ms budget'. That suggests general store latency at the time rather than a spill-specific fault. Not proven.\n\nRepro hint: emit a scorecard of about 8KB via tools:invoke under fleet load, then check _projection.cursor.reason. Suggested fix direction: make the spill write bounded or async off the response path, and add a latency metric on result-door spill writes so stalls show up in a measurement.",

          "body": "## Observed (measured 2026-09-22T19:10Z, su-4efe1c00)\nThis session's carry-respawn continuation arrived as `<pasted_content id=\"5f47\">\\n⟦turn-origin:self-compaction nonce:807623f407ac1ff3⟧ ADDRESSED TO su-4efe1c00… </pasted_content>`. The UserPromptSubmit hook stamped it `⟦turn-provenance⟧ OWNER (interactive) — no origin envelope, no ledger match` and the directive-capture rail recorded it as PENDING owner order #140 (the prior respawn's continuation had likewise become #128). Both were dismissed by me as machine-origin.\n\n## Fleet-wide scale (measured, orders:list open:true at 19:12Z)\n16 open orders; the carry excerpts of #127, #128, #130, #132, #134, #135 (self-compaction), #131, #133 (wake-pump) and #136, #137 (fleet-kickoff, recorded by role-* grading auditors) all begin `<pasted_content id=…>\\n⟦turn-origin:…⟧` — i.e. machine-injected turns captured as owner directives, ~10 in ~20 minutes across ~9 sessions.\n\n## Cause (measured in code)\n`packages/operator-core/lib/turn-provenance/envelope-grammar.ts:67` — `ENVELOPE_PATTERN_SOURCE = ^\\s*⟦turn-origin:(…) nonce:(…)⟧` is START-anchored; `parseEnvelope` (turn-provenance.ts:149) uses it, so a `<pasted_content …>` prefix defeats the match. `grep -rl pasted_content` over scripts/, packages/operator-core/lib, apps/operator/lib → 0 files: no code unwraps the wrapper. The ledger-hash fallback also misses (wrapped text ≠ injected payload), so classify() falls through to the final OWNER branch (turn-provenance.ts:671).\n[inferred, not probed] The `<pasted_content>` wrapper is added by the Claude Code client when a long prompt is delivered as input; the injectors send a correctly-enveloped payload.\n\n## Why major\n1. Manufactures owner directives out of machine text (the WI-3532 failure class) and floods every session's Orientation with bogus PENDING directives that agents must resolve by hand.\n2. The mode-registration hook is gated on this turn classifying OWNER — a wrapped machine turn containing AUTO/ideate phrasing could register a mode as ownerDirected:true.\n3. Session search provenance (`turn_origin`) marks these turns owner-typed.\n\n## Suggested durable fix\nUnwrap a leading `<pasted_content id=…>` … `</pasted_content>` (and whatever other client wrappers exist) BEFORE envelope parse + ledger hash, in ONE shared normalizer used by all 4 grammar sites (see EI-20202332205249019 — the grammar is re-typed in 4 sites/3 languages, incl. the shell form at envelope-grammar.ts:93). Recurrence guard: a unit test in turn-provenance feeding a wrapped enveloped continuation and asserting VERIFIED AGENT-ORIGIN, plus a test that a wrapped owner paste without an envelope still classifies OWNER. Consider a one-shot sweep dismissing currently-open orders whose text starts with a wrapped envelope.\n\nRelated (different leak paths, both closed): WI-38268, WI-37908.",

A full shared root volume takes PostgreSQL down fleet-wide by preventing WAL, lock, and data-directory writes.\n\ntrend: losing 0.63 GiB/h over the last 1.0h — ETA TO FULL ~7h at this rate\n\nACTION: inspect current filesystem consumers and free space before starting disk-heavy work. This probe is detection-only; it never deletes files or restarts PostgreSQL.\n\ndf output:\n/dev/nvme0n1p2  1966788624 1941918128   4861160     100% /\n\nLARGEST RELATIONS RIGHT NOW (read at alert time, not written down — see below):\n  39.53 GiB  harness_shared.session_archive_files\n  18.21 GiB  harness_shared.session_turns\n  16.06 GiB  harness_shared.tool_invocations\n  11.84 GiB  harness_shared.session_turn_chunks\n  9.89 GiB  harness_shared.coord_thread_posts\n  6.95 GiB  harness_shared.session_turn_parts\n\nA relation flagged LIKELY TOAST BLOAT is the cheapest win available and needs no owner\ndecision: its bytes are almost entirely dead TOAST pages that plain VACUUM can never\nreturn to the OS. Confirm by comparing pg_total_relation_size(reltoastrelid) against the\nlive payload (sum a denormalized length column, or sample pg_column_size), then reclaim\nwith a rewrite. ALWAYS bound the lock, because a rewrite takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and a\nblocked one queues AHEAD of every later lock request on that table:\n  sudo -n -u postgres env PGOPTIONS='-c lock_timeout=10000' psql -p 5432 -d papercusp \\\n    -c 'VACUUM (FULL, VERBOSE, ANALYZE) <schema>.<relation>'\nMeasured 2026-09-02 (WI-2140986): that reclaimed 60.89 GiB from gateway_payload_blobs in\n55s with no contention and no data loss.\n\nINVESTIGATION RECIPE (traps verified while working WI-38595, 2026-08-14, and WI-2141004, 2026-09-02):\n1. PostgreSQL is usually NOT the consumer, despite this alarm's title — but \"not PostgreSQL\" is a HYPOTHESIS TO TEST, never a conclusion to inherit. The probe watches the VOLUME holding PGDATA, and that volume is shared with $HOME. Size PGDATA with 'sudo -n du -xsh /var/lib/postgresql/18/main' — an unprivileged du prints a SILENT '4.0K' (permission denied) rather than an error, which reads as 'Postgres is tiny' for the wrong reason. Start from the LARGEST RELATIONS block above and from a fresh directory scan; do not start from any remembered figure, including one quoted in an older issue. This step used to carry a measured example here, and it went stale and misdirected three work-items for three weeks.\n2. CONFIRM WHICH VOLUME a directory is on before reclaiming anything: 'findmnt -T <path>' or 'stat -c %d <path>'. On this box /tmp is a BIND MOUNT from a second physical disk, so deleting 136 GiB of stale /tmp scratch frees exactly nothing on the volume this alarm is about.\n3. Enumerate consumers in ONE bounded backgrounded pass: 'nice -n 19 ionice -c3 du -x -d3 / | sort -hr > /tmp/scan-1.txt' (~7 min here). Re-run it later into scan-2.txt and DIFF the two — a diff of two snapshots is the only reliable attribution of NET growth per directory.\n4. Do NOT attribute growth by mtime ('find -newermt'). It counts a file's WHOLE size when the file is merely touched, so a single live VM image reads as hundreds of GiB 'written' in 26h. Note also that qcow2 images grow monotonically and never return space the guest frees — and the .img suffix lies, so check the magic ('QFI\\373' = qcow2).",
